title: Heat, Temperature, and Thermal Energy
description: What heat actually is — and why it flows the way it does

concepts.title: Temperature vs Heat
concepts.contentHtml:
Temperature and heat are not the same thing. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. Heat is the energy transferred between objects because of a temperature difference.

A bathtub of lukewarm water contains far more thermal energy than a lit match — but the match is hotter. This distinction matters enormously in engineering and cooking alike.

Temperature is measured in kelvin (K), Celsius (°C), or Fahrenheit (°F). The absolute zero of the kelvin scale (0 K = −273.15 °C) is the lowest possible temperature, where thermal motion reaches its minimum (quantum zero-point motion still remains).

concepts.title: Thermal Energy and Specific Heat
concepts.contentHtml:
When you heat an object, you add energy to it. The amount of energy needed depends on the substance's specific heat capacity (c) — how much energy per kilogram per degree of temperature rise.

Water has an unusually high specific heat (4,186 J/kg·K), which is why oceans moderate coastal climates and why water is used as a coolant.

The heat transfer equation Q = mcΔT relates heat added (Q) to mass (m), specific heat (c), and temperature change (ΔT). Double the mass or double the temperature rise and you need double the energy.

concepts.title: Modes of Heat Transfer
concepts.contentHtml:
Heat moves by three mechanisms:

Conduction: direct contact transfers vibrations between adjacent particles. Metals conduct well; wood and air do not. This is why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature — it draws heat from your hand faster.

Convection: hot fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, creating circulation loops. Responsible for ocean currents, wind, and boiling water.

Radiation: electromagnetic waves carry energy through empty space — no medium needed. The Sun heats Earth by radiation across 150 million kilometres of vacuum.

title: The Four Laws of Thermodynamics
description: Nature's ironclad rules about energy and its transformations

concepts.title: Zeroth and First Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
The Zeroth Law formalises the notion of temperature: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A and C are also in equilibrium. This seems obvious — but it's the logical foundation for thermometers to exist at all.

The First Law is conservation of energy for thermal systems: the change in internal energy of a system equals heat added minus work done by the system.

ΔU = Q − W. If you add 100 J of heat and the gas does 40 J of work by expanding, its internal energy rises by 60 J. Energy is never created or destroyed.

concepts.title: Second Law — Entropy Always Increases
concepts.contentHtml:
The Second Law is one of the most profound in all of science: in any spontaneous process, the total entropy of the universe never decreases.

Heat flows from hot to cold, not the reverse. Perfume spreads through a room but never spontaneously reconcentrates. These are the Second Law in action.

No process can be 100% efficient at converting heat to work. Some energy is always 'wasted' as low-grade heat. This limits steam engines, power plants, and refrigerators alike.

concepts.title: Third Law — Absolute Zero
concepts.contentHtml:
The Third Law: as a system approaches absolute zero (0 K), its entropy approaches a constant minimum (usually zero for a perfect crystal).

This means it's impossible to reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps — you can get arbitrarily close but never there. Modern labs have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a kelvin of absolute zero using laser cooling and evaporative cooling techniques.

The Third Law also allows us to calculate absolute entropies rather than just entropy changes — essential in chemistry for predicting reaction spontaneity.

title: Entropy and the Arrow of Time
description: Why disorder increases and time only moves forward

concepts.title: Boltzmann's Statistical Definition of Entropy
concepts.contentHtml:
Ludwig Boltzmann gave entropy a microscopic meaning in 1877. Entropy S is proportional to the logarithm of the number of microstates Ω — the number of different arrangements of particles that give the same macroscopic state.

S = k_B ln Ω, where k_B is Boltzmann's constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K).

A hot gas concentrated in one corner has few microstates (low Ω, low S). Spread throughout the room, the number of arrangements explodes — entropy is overwhelmingly higher. Systems evolve toward high-entropy states simply because there are vastly more of them.

concepts.title: The Arrow of Time
concepts.contentHtml:
The fundamental equations of physics — Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations, even quantum mechanics — are time-symmetric. Run them backward and they remain valid. Yet we experience time as having a direction: eggs break but don't reassemble; coffee cools but doesn't heat up spontaneously.

The resolution is entropy. The past had lower entropy than the present. Entropy's tendency to increase is what defines the 'arrow' of time — past = lower entropy, future = higher entropy.

This deep connection between thermodynamics and time is still an active area of research, tied to the conditions at the Big Bang.

concepts.title: Entropy and Information
concepts.contentHtml:
Shannon's information entropy (1948) and Boltzmann's thermodynamic entropy are mathematically identical in form. This is not a coincidence.

Erasing a bit of information necessarily dissipates at least k_B T ln 2 of energy as heat — Landauer's principle. Computation has a fundamental thermodynamic cost.

Maxwell's Demon — a thought experiment of a tiny creature that could sort fast and slow molecules — seemed to violate the Second Law. The resolution: the demon must store and erase information, and that erasure generates exactly enough entropy to compensate. Information is physical.

title: Heat Engines and Refrigerators
description: Turning heat into work — and the limits of efficiency

concepts.title: Heat Engines and the Carnot Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
A heat engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, converts some to useful work, and dumps the rest into a cold reservoir. Sadi Carnot proved in 1824 that the maximum possible efficiency depends only on the temperatures of the two reservoirs.

The Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot (in kelvin). A steam turbine with steam at 600 K and cooling water at 300 K has a Carnot efficiency of 50%. Real engines fall below this theoretical maximum due to friction, heat leaks, and irreversibilities.

No engine operating between two fixed temperatures can exceed Carnot efficiency — this follows directly from the Second Law.

concepts.title: Refrigerators and Heat Pumps
concepts.contentHtml:
A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: it uses work to pump heat from a cold interior to a warm room. This doesn't violate the Second Law because work is being supplied from outside.

The coefficient of performance (COP) for a refrigerator = Q_cold / W. For a Carnot refrigerator: COP = T_C / (T_H − T_C). The closer the temperatures, the less work needed — which is why fridges work harder in hot kitchens.

A heat pump heats a building by pumping heat from cold outside air indoors. It can deliver more heat energy than the electrical energy consumed — COP > 1 — making it more efficient than direct electric heating.

concepts.title: Real Engines: Steam, Otto, Diesel
concepts.contentHtml:
Real engines approximate idealised thermodynamic cycles:

Steam (Rankine) cycle: used in power plants and steam locomotives — water boils to steam, expands through a turbine, condenses, and is pumped back.

Otto cycle: petrol car engines — four strokes (intake, compression, power, exhaust) approximate adiabatic and isochoric processes.

Diesel cycle: compression ratio is higher (18:1 vs 8:1), no spark plug — air gets so hot from compression that injected diesel ignites spontaneously. Higher compression → higher efficiency.

All real engines lose efficiency to friction, incomplete combustion, and heat losses to engine walls.

title: Thermodynamics at the Frontier
description: Black hole thermodynamics, Maxwell's Demon, and the heat death of the universe

concepts.title: Black Hole Thermodynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking discovered that black holes obey laws analogous to thermodynamics. A black hole has:

— Temperature (Hawking temperature): T_H = ℏc³ / (8πGMk_B). Smaller black holes are hotter and evaporate faster.
— Entropy proportional to its event horizon area: S = k_B A / (4 l_P²), where l_P is the Planck length.

The entropy of a black hole is enormous — a solar-mass black hole has entropy ~10⁷⁷ k_B. This horizon-area entropy is the deepest clue we have about quantum gravity and the holographic principle.

concepts.title: Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics and Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical thermodynamics described systems near equilibrium. Real life — literally — operates far from equilibrium. Living organisms import low-entropy energy (food, sunlight) and export high-entropy waste (heat, carbon dioxide), locally decreasing their own entropy while increasing the universe's total.

Ilya Prigogine won the 1977 Nobel Prize for showing that far-from-equilibrium systems can spontaneously self-organise into ordered dissipative structures — convection cells, chemical oscillations, and ultimately life itself.

The Second Law does not forbid local order; it requires that global disorder increase. Life is not magic — it's a very sophisticated entropy export machine.

concepts.title: The Heat Death of the Universe
concepts.contentHtml:
If the Second Law holds forever, the universe tends toward maximum entropy — a cold, uniform, featureless state called the heat death. All temperature gradients vanish; no work can be extracted; no complexity can persist.

On a timescale of ~10¹⁰⁰ years, all black holes will evaporate via Hawking radiation. After that, only a dilute soup of photons and leptons remains, expanding and cooling toward absolute zero forever.

Whether quantum gravity, or some unforeseen physics, alters this fate is unknown. The heat death is the ultimate consequence of the Second Law applied to the whole cosmos — the most profound implication of a simple laboratory observation about steam engines.

title: Statistical Foundations
description: Where the laws of thermodynamics actually come from

concepts.title: Microstates and Macrostates
concepts.contentHtml:
A macrostate is what you measure: temperature, pressure, volume. A microstate is the exact position and momentum of every molecule.

An astronomical number of microstates correspond to any given macrostate — typically e^(N) of them, where N ≈ 10²³ is Avogadro's number.

Boltzmann's insight: entropy is a count. S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω is the number of microstates compatible with the macrostate. The Second Law becomes a statistical truism — overwhelmingly likely macrostates have overwhelming numbers of microstates.

concepts.title: The Boltzmann Distribution
concepts.contentHtml:
For a system in thermal equilibrium with a reservoir at temperature T, the probability of finding it in a state of energy E is proportional to e^(-E/k_B T) — the Boltzmann distribution.

High-energy states are exponentially suppressed at low T. As T increases, more states are accessible. This single formula underlies chemical reaction rates (Arrhenius), atmospheric density profiles, and the speed distribution of molecules in a gas.

concepts.title: Equipartition
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical statistical mechanics gives every quadratic degree of freedom (a kinetic or potential mode that appears as ½αx² in the energy) an average energy of ½ k_B T at temperature T.

Three translational degrees of freedom for a monoatomic gas → 3/2 k_B T per molecule, hence c_V = 3/2 R per mole. Diatomic molecules add rotational modes; vibrational modes only kick in at high T (at lower T, quantum effects freeze them out).

The departure from classical equipartition was one of the first hints that quantum mechanics was needed.

concepts.title: First-Order Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Boiling water and freezing ice are first-order phase transitions. Energy (latent heat) must be added or removed at a specific temperature for the transition to proceed; the temperature pauses while the change happens.

Two phases coexist at the transition: liquid and gas, or liquid and solid. The chemical potentials of the two phases are equal.

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates how the transition temperature varies with pressure. It explains why pressure cookers work (water boils hotter under pressure) and why ice skating works (high pressure under skates lowers the melting point — though that explanation has been challenged).

concepts.title: Continuous Transitions and Critical Points
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometimes transitions happen smoothly. Approach the critical point of water (374 °C, 218 atm) and the distinction between liquid and gas vanishes — density fluctuations become huge, the substance turns milky (critical opalescence), and you cross from liquid to gas without any latent heat.

Continuous transitions also describe ferromagnetism (Curie point), superconductivity onset, and superfluidity. Universality classes link wildly different physical systems through their critical exponents.

concepts.title: Beyond Liquid-Gas-Solid
concepts.contentHtml:
Real matter is more inventive. Plasmas, superfluids, Bose-Einstein condensates, liquid crystals, supercritical fluids — each is a distinct phase with its own thermodynamic behaviour.

Modern condensed-matter physics has expanded the catalogue: topological phases, quantum spin liquids, fractional quantum Hall states. Some of these aren't characterized by symmetry breaking at all but by topology.

concepts.title: Maxwell's Demon
concepts.contentHtml:
James Clerk Maxwell imagined (1867) a tiny intelligent being controlling a door between two gas chambers. The demon lets fast molecules go one way and slow ones the other, separating hot from cold without any work — apparently violating the Second Law.

For a century, this was a paradox. Resolution: the demon's information about molecule speeds is not free. To act, then erase its memory to start over, requires entropy production at least equal to what it saves.

concepts.title: Landauer's Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Rolf Landauer (1961): erasing one bit of information at temperature T requires at least k_B T ln 2 of dissipated energy. This is the fundamental thermodynamic cost of irreversible computation.

The bound has been verified experimentally. Reversible computation could in principle approach zero dissipation per logic operation — the field of reversible computing explores this limit.

Modern computers dissipate about 10⁹ k_B T per bit erased — vast room before the Landauer limit becomes a hard ceiling, but the gap is closing.

concepts.title: Information Is Physical
concepts.contentHtml:
Landauer's slogan, drilled into computer scientists ever since. The physical state of any information storage — patterns of magnetization, electron occupancy, DNA sequence — has thermodynamic consequences.

This connection ripples outward: the Bekenstein bound limits information density in any region of space; black hole entropy limits how much information a region of spacetime can hold. The deepest law of thermodynamics may be: information has a cost, always.
